senses.d: A portal of entry into a building, room, or vehicle, typically consisting of a rigid plane movable on a hinge. It may have a handle to help open and close, a latch to hold it closed, and a lock that ensures it cannot be opened without a key.
ex: bathroom door, bedroom door, doorkey, exterior door, interior door
I knocked on the vice president's door.

senses.d: A building with a door, especially a house.
ex: His house is three doors down.
He went five doors up the road to the bank.

senses.d: Any flap, etc., that opens like a door.
ex: cupboard door
the 24 doors in an Advent calendar

senses.d: An entry point.
A means of approach or access.
ex: Learning is the door to wisdom.

senses.d: A possibility.
ex: to leave the door open
all doors are open to somebody

senses.d: A barrier.
ex: Keep a door on your anger.

senses.d: A software mechanism by which a user can interact with a program running remotely on a bulletin board system. See BBS door.
The proceeds from entrance fees and/or ticket sales at a venue such as a bar or nightclub, especially in relation to portion paid to the entertainers.
ex: The bar owner gives each band a percentage of the door and charges customers more to get in.

senses.d: To cause a collision by opening the door of a vehicle in front of an oncoming cyclist or pedestrian.

From Middle English doom, dom, from Old English dōm (“judgement”), from Proto-West Germanic *dōm, from Proto-Germanic *dōmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰóh₁mos. Cognates Compare Dutch doem (“condemnation, doom; judgement”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish dom (“judgement”), Faroese and Icelandic dómur (“judgement”), Gothic 𐌳𐍉𐌼𐍃 (dōms, “insight, judgement”); also Ancient Greek θωμός (thōmós, “heap”), Bulgarian, Macedonian, Russian, and Ukrainian ду́ма (dúma, “thought”), Polish duma (“pride”). Doublet of duma. See also deem.

senses.d: Destiny, especially terrible.
ex: This, for the night; by day, the web and loom, / And homely houſhold-taſk, ſhall be her doom,
"When should I expect him?" Roy said, resigned to his doom.

senses.d: An undesirable fate; an impending severe occurrence or danger that seems inevitable.
ex: Chung was the first of its four picks in Round 2. His arrival might spell doom for Rodney Harrison.

senses.d: Dread; a feeling of danger, impending danger, darkness, or despair.
ex: I'm taking medications every day; never thinking I would be spiraling into nothing but a nightmare that made me feel doom.
Then the smiling narrator filled me with doom: I was expected to pull my own rip cord. I nearly fainted.

senses.d: A law.
A judgment or decision.
ex: And there he learned of things and haps to come, / To give foreknowledge true, and certain doom.
But the day of doome shall be the end of this time, and the beginning of the immortality for to come, wherein corruption is past.

senses.d: A sentence or penalty for illegal behaviour.
ex: The first dooms of London provide especially the recovery of cattle belonging to the citizens.
Appeals were by our ancient law styled falsing of dooms. They were to be entered immediately after doom or sentence was pronounced,

senses.d: Death.
ex: They met an untimely doom when the mineshaft caved in.
This is the day of doom for Bassianus.

senses.d: The Last Judgment; or, an artistic representation thereof.
To pronounce judgment or sentence on; to condemn.
ex: a criminal doomed to death
Absolves the just, and dooms the guilty souls.

senses.d: To destine; to fix irrevocably the ill fate of.
ex: A man of genius […] doomed to struggle with difficulties.

senses.d: To judge; to estimate or determine as a judge.
ex: And while we know not that the King of heaven hath not doomed this place our safe retreat

senses.d: To ordain as a penalty; hence, to mulct or fine.
ex: Have I tongue to doom my brother's death?

senses.d: To assess a tax upon, by estimate or at discretion.
To be extremely pessimistic about something.
ex: Every time I see people dooming over North America I just assume its because they've never seen the parts of it that look like this

ex: I stood by the doorway to watch her go.

senses.d: An opening or passage in general.
ex: Soon after dawn, he came to the doorway of my tent.

senses.d: An outside step leading up to the door of a building, usually a home.
ex: Ailie was standing by the doorstep as he came down the road, and her heart stood still with joy.

senses.d: One's immediate neighborhood or locality.
ex: They want to build the prison right on our doorstep; it will only be half a mile away and being that close scares me.

senses.d: A thick slice, especially of bread.
ex: I cut myself a doorstep of bread with masses of butter and went along to see Romanov while I was eating it.
